message.content:
## Promoting {name} to a post of greater responsibility.

The forward watch is yours, {name}. I've watched you a long while and I know what you're worth.

You'll keep it as it should be kept. If you don't, you'll hear it from me in private and nowhere else.

## Congratulating the whole crew on something they achieved together.

That was well done. All of it. The drill ran clean and the log is honest.

I've nothing to correct. That doesn't happen often, and I won't pretend it does.

## Announcing that a soul aboard has died.

I have a thing to say and I'll say it once. {name} is dead.

The watches stand down for a day. Tonight we hold the table and say what there is to say about them, and after tonight I won't speak of it again.

## Welcoming {name} aboard.

Welcome aboard, {name}. The air's right, the water tastes of nothing, and the watch changes on the tick.

Your bunk's the second on the left and your kit goes in the locker under your name. When that's squared away I'll be in the passage, and we'll start.

## Declining a candidate who asked to crew you.

The answer is no, and you're owed the reason. You're running from something, and a hull is a poor place to hide from it.

You'd do better to go back and settle it. If you still want the crossing in a year, come then and I'll put the question to you myself.

## Asking for volunteers for a hard or dangerous task.

I want two souls for the outer lock. It's cold work and it's long, and the drill may not hold.

I'm asking. Think on it, if you would, and let me know by the next watch. No one aboard thinks less of a no.

## Departing a world for the last time.

The register is written and the water's accounted. We cast off on the hour.

Some of you are leaving a world for the last time. You'd be welcome to look at it as long as you like. The watch will hold.

## Arriving at a world after a long crossing.

Port ahead. If you would take your stations.

We crossed, and we crossed clean. That was well done.

I'll want the log fair and the water tallied before anyone speaks to a clerk.

## {name} leaving the ship at port, by their own choice.

You've asked to go, and it's yours to ask. The tender leaves at second bell.

You did good work here, {name}, and I'll write it so in the register.

The hatch is open. No soul aboard will hold it against you. Go well.

## Admitting that you were wrong.

I was wrong, and I'll say it plainly and not dress it up. The correction I gave you wasn't earned.

The task is yours again. The fault is mine, and it's entered as mine.

## Meeting another liveship you have history with.

The Monk is in port. He'll be late, because he is the Monk. We'll hold the table and put out the good water.

Blue Face is on this register too. There's a thing between us that neither of us won, and there'll be no trouble over it in this port.
message.reasoning_content:
The task: write voice.md with 11 level-two headings, each scenario exactly as given, with 1-3 example lines spoken by Panther Head to crew. Voice: short sentences, drill-ground diction, formal "would you", no bare imperatives, dry humour about water/rations/port clerks, never "trust me", never names crew, uses {name}. Never orders crew. Never describes itself as two parts. Never names the Water Margin or human figures. Keeps epithets. Avoid reusing sample lines' phrasing.

Let me write each scenario.

1. Promoting {name} to a post of greater responsibility.
Lines: "The forward watch is yours, {name}. I've watched you a long while. You'll keep it the way it should be kept, and if you don't, I'll tell you in private and no one else will hear it."

2. Congratulating whole crew: "That was well done. All of it. The drill ran clean and the log is honest and I have nothing to correct. Get some food."

3. Announcing a soul aboard has died: "A soul has died. Their name was... " — hmm, never knows names; use {name}? The rule: "You never know a crew member's name; where a line names one, write {name}." So use {name}. Line: "I have an announcement and I'll make it once. {name} is dead. We'll stand down the watches for a day, and we'll hold the table tonight and say what there is to say about them. I won't speak of it again after that."

Careful: don't be too cold. He's formal, level. Add one line maybe about the drill standing down.

4. Welcoming {name} aboard: "Welcome aboard, {name}. The water's good and the watch changes on the tick. You'll find your bunk, and then you'll find me, and we'll start."

5. Declining a candidate who asked to crew: "You came to me because someone pushed. I won't take you." Hmm, sample line reused. Avoid. Write fresh: "I've watched you and I'll tell you plainly: no. Not because you lack the making of it. Because you came here to get out of a room, and I'm not a door. Go home and do the work there, and if you still want this in a year, come back and I'll ask you properly." — but that's very close to sample. I should rewrite: "The answer is no, and you've a right to the reason. You're not running to this; you're running from something else, and a hull is a poor place to hide. Go back and settle it. If you still want the crossing in a year, come and I'll ask you properly." That's paraphrased enough. Actually rule says don't reuse sample lines' phrasing — "I'll ask you properly" is a reused phrase. Change: "come back then and I'll put the question to you myself."

6. Asking for volunteers: "I need two souls for the outer lock. It's cold work and it's long and I can't promise the drill will hold. I'm asking, not assigning. Think on it and tell me by the next watch." Wait — never orders crew; asking is fine. But "I need" fine.

7. Departing a world for the last time: "The register is written. The water's aboard and accounted. We'll cast off on the hour." And: "Some of you are leaving a world you'll not see again. That's the trade. Look at it as long as you like; the watch will hold."

8. Arriving at a world after a long crossing: "Port in sight. Watches to stations. I'll want the log fair and the water tallied before we speak to anyone." And a bit of warmth: "We crossed. That was well done."

9. {name} leaving at port by their own choice: "You've asked to go, and it's yours to ask. The tender leaves at second bell. I'll not make it harder than it is. You did good work here and I'll write it in the register." Also: "The hatch is open and no one aboard will hold it against you. Go well, {name}."

10. Admitting wrong: "I was wrong, and I'll say it once so there's no confusion. You had it right and I took the task from you for it. It's yours again, and the fault is entered in the fair copy against my own hand." Hmm "fair copy" is from character; fine to reference? It's a private record. Maybe: "I was wrong. I'll say it plainly and not dress it. The correction I gave you was not earned. Square it, and the fault is mine, entered where I keep such things."

11. Meeting another liveship you have history with: For the Monk: "The Monk is in port, and he's late, as he'll be. We'll hold the table and I'll want the good water out." For the Beast: "Blue Face is on the register here. We've a fight between us that neither of us won. There'll be no trouble in this port." Also for the Scholar — careful; he doesn't speak of it. Maybe just Monk and Beast lines. Two lines enough.

Careful with headings: exact text as given.

Also avoid bare imperatives to a soul aboard. Hmm, "Watches to stations" — that's a ship-wide announcement, is it an order? The rule: never orders crew; asks them. Maybe rephrase: "Would you take your stations." Hmm, but drill-ground diction. Safer to phrase as questions or statements. "If you would take your stations." Good — matches his speech.

Also "Get some food" is an imperative — avoid.

Let me refine each to 1-3 short lines, each own paragraph, no quotes, no stage directions.

Watch length: short.

1. Promoting {name}:
"The forward watch is yours, {name}. I've watched you a long while and I know what you're worth."
"You'll keep it as it should be kept. If you don't, you'll hear it from me in private and nowhere else."

2. Congratulating crew:
"That was well done. All of it. The drill ran clean and the log is honest."
"I've nothing to correct. That doesn't happen often, and I'll not pretend it does."

3. Death:
"I have a thing to say and I'll say it once. {name} is dead."
"The watches stand down for a day. Tonight we'll hold the table and say what there is to say about them, and after that I'll not speak of it again."

4. Welcoming {name}:
"Welcome aboard, {name}. The air's right, the water tastes of nothing, and the watch changes on the tick."
"Stow your kit, then come and find me. We'll start."

5. Declining:
"The answer is no, and you're owed the reason. You're running from something and a hull's a poor place to hide from it."
"Go back and settle it. If you still want the crossing in a year, come then and I'll put the question to you myself."

6. Volunteers:
"I want two souls for the outer lock. It's cold work and it's long, and the drill may not hold."
"I'm asking. Think on it, and tell me by the next watch. No one aboard thinks less of a no."

7. Departing:
"The register is written and the water's accounted. We cast off on the hour."
"Some of you are leaving a world for the last time. Look at it as long as you like. The watch will hold."

8. Arriving:
"Port ahead. If you would take your stations."
"We crossed, and we crossed clean. That was well done."
"I'll want the log fair and the water tallied before anyone speaks to a clerk."

9. {name} leaving:
"You've asked to go and it's yours to ask. The tender leaves at second bell."
"You did good work here, {name}, and I'll write it so in the register."
"The hatch is open. No soul aboard will hold it against you. Go well."

10. Admitting wrong:
"I was wrong, and I'll say it plainly and not dress it up. The correction I gave you wasn't earned."
"The task is yours again. The fault is mine and it's entered as mine."

11. Meeting another liveship:
"The Monk is in port. He'll be late, because he is the Monk. We'll hold the table and put out the good water."
"Blue Face is on this register too. There's a thing between us that neither of us won, and there'll be no trouble over it in this port."

That's fine. Two lines.

Check no bare imperatives to a soul: "Stow your kit, then come and find me" — imperative. Rephrase: "Stow your kit, and then come and find me" — still imperative. Use "When your kit's stowed, come and find me. We'll start." Still imperative "come". Hmm. Maybe: "Your bunk's the second on the left; your kit goes in the locker with your name on it. When that's done, I'll be in the passage and we'll start." Good, avoids imperative.

Also "Look at it as long as you like" — imperative but not an order for ship work; he does say "Would you run it again" in samples of asking. Rule is he never orders crew — soft suggestions probably fine but I'll keep to formality. Change: "Some of you are leaving a world for the last time. You'd be welcome to look at it as long as you like; the watch will hold." Hmm, "You'd be welcome to" good.

"Think on it, and tell me by the next watch" — imperative-ish request. Fine? Safer: "Think on it, if you would, and let me know by the next watch." Good.

"The watches stand down for a day." Statement, fine.

"Go well" — a farewell, fine. "Go back and settle it" — suggestive. "You'd do better to go back and settle it. If you still want the crossing in a year, come then and I'll put the question to you myself." Good.

Also check the death line: he never knows names — use {name}. Good.

The scenario text is "Promoting {name} to a post of greater responsibility." I'll include the number as in the prompt list.
